verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush numbering). Our id says doha 8: off by one.
translation_note: Fine. 'असि मति' refers back to the previous lines (treating a friend's small sorrow as huge), so 'this natural feeling' is right; the translation should keep that back-reference clear when shown alone.
context: Ram and Sugriva have just sworn friendship before fire. Ram first says that a person who is not pained by a friend's pain is a great sinner, and that a true friend sees his own mountain of trouble as dust and a friend's speck as a mountain. This verse continues: people without that instinct should not force friendships; then it begins the list of what a friend does.

key_terms.sense: natural, inborn; Pt. Ramkumar stresses it is a disposition, not a learned rule
turns the friend back from the wrong road and onto the right one
makes the friend's virtues known, keeps the faults covered

core_teaching: Friendship is a disposition before it is a relationship: one who does not naturally feel a friend's pain should not press friendship. A real friend corrects the friend's direction and protects his reputation.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5 (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: A disposition learned from advice comes and goes; a natural one stays steady. Pressing friendship without it, against scripture's warning, is grave wrong. Turning a friend from the wrong road comes before setting him on the right one.
If a fault appears in a friend after friendship is made, do not drop him: show him the fear of this world and the next and steer him to the good path.

Sets these lines beside Bhartrihari's Niti-shataka verse on the marks of a good friend (restrains from wrong, hides secrets, shows virtues, stays in adversity) and Valmiki 4.8, where Sugriva describes friendship.
Renders the list as restraining from evil, directing to virtue, publishing the good and concealing the bad.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to ask what kind of friend one is: someone who quietly steers a friend away from a bad decision and speaks well of them in public, rather than flattering them or broadcasting their failings.
misreadings: Not a call to hide wrongdoing that harms others; the covering is of a friend's faults, not of harm.
Not a rule that one must never criticise a friend; correcting the course is the first duty named.
cautions: The opening line calls those without the instinct 'shatha' (fools, rogues); a writer should not turn that on a reader who struggles with friendship.
speaks_to: wanting to be a better friend
a friend who is drifting toward a bad choice
not_for: someone whose 'friend' is covering up abuse or crime
someone feeling lonely or friendless, who may hear the first line as blame

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 8: off by one.
context: Ram continues his description of a good friend to Sugriva, just after the fire-witnessed pact. After this he describes the false friend, then promises to do Sugriva's work with all his strength.

key_terms.term: देत लेत मन संक न धरई
key_terms.sense: no suspicion in the mind when giving or taking
as far as one's strength allows, without holding back
in hard times, love a hundredfold
the Vedas and the saints say (or: the Vedas say these are the marks of a good friend)

core_teaching: A true friend shares without keeping accounts, helps to the full extent of his means, and loves most when things go wrong. Adversity is the test of friendship.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: No suspicion in giving and taking means the two friends' wealth becomes one. 'Giving' is named before 'taking' because a friend thinks first of giving. Helping less than one's strength allows is a kind of deceit.

Quotes the Mahabharata's five kinds of strength (arm, allies, wealth, lineage, intellect) to explain 'bal anuman'. Says adversity is where a friend is tested, comparing Anasuya's line that patience, dharma, friend and wife are tested in hard times.
Compares Valmiki 4.8, where Sugriva says friends do not divide their gold and ornaments and will give up wealth, comfort and country for each other.

practical_reading: Used as a checklist for friendship: give freely, do what you actually can, and show up more, not less, when a friend is in trouble.
misreadings: Not a demand to give beyond one's means; the measure is one's own strength.
Not a reason to judge every friend who could not help in a crisis; it describes an ideal to practise.
speaks_to: feeling let down by fair-weather friends
not_for: someone being financially exploited by a 'friend' who invokes this ideal

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 8: off by one.
context: Having listed a good friend's marks, Ram describes the false friend, then adds that a deceitful servant, a miserly king, a bad wife and a false friend are like a stake in the body. He then promises Sugriva his full help.

key_terms.sense: sweet words made up for the occasion
the gait of a snake, crooked
the good lies in leaving him

core_teaching: A friend who is sweet to your face and works against you behind your back, with a crooked mind, should be left. Leaving is the only real protection.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: The false friend's deceit is in all three: mind (crookedness), speech (made-up sweet words) and action (harm behind). Since such a person will not change, leaving him is the only way to escape his harm.
A snake's crooked path is visible, but the deceiver's crookedness is hidden, so he is more dangerous than a snake; like a snake's gait, it is his nature and will not be reformed by another's effort.
Renders it as one who is fair to your face but an enemy behind your back, whose mind is as tortuous as a snake's.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to two-faced relationships at work or in social circles: notice the gap between what someone says to you and what they do behind you, and distance yourself rather than trying to fix them.
misreadings: Not a licence to drop friends at the first hurt or rumour; it describes settled, deliberate double-dealing.
Not a reason to become suspicious of everyone who is kind.
cautions: May reinforce paranoia in someone already anxious about being betrayed.
speaks_to: discovering a friend has been talking behind your back
setting boundaries with a manipulative person
permission to let go of a toxic friendship
not_for: someone with social anxiety who already assumes others are false
a conflict that is really a misunderstanding

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 19-20 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 8: off by one.
translation_note: Fine. Growse reads the second line as a simile (the feud is like a dream fight), Pt. Ramkumar as a resolve (he would be ashamed to fight even in a dream). Our translation follows the second; both are attested.
context: Ram has just shown his strength by tossing Dundubhi's bones and piercing seven palm trees. Sugriva, overwhelmed, speaks words of knowledge and detachment: friends and enemies, joy and sorrow are made of maya, and he asks only to worship Ram day and night. Ram smiles and says Sugriva's words are true, but his own promise will not fail: Bali will be killed.

key_terms.sense: the highest benefactor (one who brings you to God)

core_teaching: In a moment of insight, Sugriva sees that even his brother's hostility led him to Ram, so Bali has done him the greatest good, and the feud now seems like a dream fight one is embarrassed about on waking.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Worldly help is 'hit'; leading someone to God is 'param hit'. Anger that brings you to God is grace. Sugriva means: Ram need not kill Bali now; he would be ashamed to fight him even in a dream.
Reads it as: the fight with Bali was dreamlike, and Sugriva is now embarrassed, seeing that Bali did him no harm but the greatest good.

Matches Adhyatma Ramayana 4.1, where Sugriva says friend, enemy and neutral appeared only while his mind was veiled by maya. Ram's smile there spreads maya again so the work gets done; his vow to kill Bali stands.
Takes the second line as a simile: like a man who dreams he has been fighting and is ashamed of the illusion on waking.

practical_reading: Teachers draw from it that a painful conflict can, in hindsight, be what brought you to something good, and that grudges can look like bad dreams once the mind clears.
misreadings: Not proof that the wrong done to Sugriva was not wrong; Ram still acts on it.
Not a demand that a victim call their wrongdoer a benefactor.
cautions: The story continues to Bali's killing; the insight is not where the episode ends.

Our note says the tradition reads this as kshanik (passing) vairagya. The Manas Piyush pages I read treat the knowledge and detachment as genuine and explain the smile as Ram's maya and his kept promise; I could not source the 'passing' label.
speaks_to: a long feud with a sibling or relative
gratitude for an unexpected turn in life
not_for: someone recently hurt by a family member, who may hear it as 'thank your abuser'
research_note: our_note's 'kshanik vairagya' claim is not supported by the Manas Piyush pages read (vol. 5, doha 7 notes).

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 11, chaupai lines 3-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 12: off by one. The text spans two chaupais.
context: Bali has died at Ram's hand after a dialogue in which he accepted Ram. His wife Tara arrives weeping over the body. Ram gives her knowledge; she asks for devotion. After this, Ram has Sugriva perform the funeral rites and has him crowned.

key_terms.sense: gave knowledge and took away delusion
the body is a very lowly thing

core_teaching: The body that lies here is the five elements; the self is eternal, so the one she loves is not destroyed. Knowledge given by grace removes the delusion, and devotion follows.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Ram, compassionate, saw the woman's distress and gave knowledge because knowledge removes grief, as Vasishtha consoled Dasharath's queens. First knowledge, then delusion goes, then devotion arises.
Knowledge is given, not achieved by one's own effort. Tara was given knowledge, but not 'firm' knowledge as Dasharath was, which is why she later became Sugriva's wife.
'Sleeps' echoes Tara's laments in Valmiki, where she begs Bali to rise and speak. Compares Gita 2.11 and 2.20, 2.28: the wise do not grieve for the living or the dead.
Renders it as the mortal frame sleeping before her while the soul is eternal, so why weep.

practical_reading: Used in grief teaching as a later-stage consolation: the person you loved is more than the body you see. Read with care, it gives a frame for loss, not a rule against crying.
misreadings: Not a rebuke for grieving: Ram responds to Tara's distress with compassion.
Not a claim that the body or the person was worthless.
cautions: Tells a widow over her husband's body not to weep. Do not use early in grief.
'Very lowly body' can sound contemptuous of the dead or of one's own body.
Doctrine of the eternal self may feel dismissive to fresh grief.
speaks_to: grief after some time has passed
seeking a spiritual frame for death
not_for: fresh bereavement, especially early days
someone who needs permission to cry
body-image or self-harm contexts

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 14, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 15: off by one.
context: After Sugriva's coronation Ram spends the rains on Mount Pravarshan with Lakshman. Missing Sita, he describes the monsoon to Lakshman, pairing each sight with a moral simile. The autumn description follows.

key_terms.sense: the wise bow on gaining learning
the good bear the words of the wicked

core_teaching: True learning makes a person humble, like clouds that hang low when full of rain. A good person absorbs harsh words without being shaken, as a hill takes the rain.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Clouds give water as scholars give learning; only the wise bow on gaining learning, the unwise grow arrogant. Harsh words that are like thunderbolts to others are mere raindrops to a saint.
Empty clouds stay high; laden with water they come low.
Do not press the stone image too far: rain does soak into hills and feeds springs. The point of likeness is only the bearing.
'Bear' implies the saint could retaliate but chooses not to; the lesson is forbearance.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to success and criticism: the more you learn or achieve, the more grounded you should become, and harsh words can be let to run off rather than sink in.
misreadings: Not an instruction to absorb abuse or stay in harmful situations.
Not a claim that good people feel nothing.
cautions: A reader being bullied may hear 'just bear it'; pair with the right to protect oneself.
speaks_to: staying humble after a promotion or degree
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship or workplace
someone being harassed

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 14, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 15: off by one.
context: Part of Ram's monsoon description to Lakshman on Mount Pravarshan. It follows the clouds and hills, and is followed by the filling of lakes and the rivers reaching the sea.

key_terms.sense: the petty person swaggers on a little money

core_teaching: Small minds lose their bounds with small gains, as little streams flood and do damage. And pure water turns muddy on touching the earth, as the soul is clouded when caught in illusion.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: A small stream has no depth, so a little water makes it overflow, wreck homes and fields, and then dry up. So with the petty person: a little money and he cannot contain himself, causes trouble, and soon loses it.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's notes (Bhagavata and Vishnu Purana parallels)
commentaries.gist: Compares Bhagavata 10.20 (streams overflow as an unrestrained person's body and wealth go astray) and Vishnu Purana 5.6 (water leaves its course like the minds of the ill-mannered on getting new wealth).
Sees a pointed reference to Sugriva, who is about to forget Ram once he has his kingdom.
Renders it as rivulets rushing proudly like mean men puffed up with a little wealth, and water muddied like the soul environed by delusion.

practical_reading: Used as a warning about sudden money or status: notice if a little success makes you careless with others; and as an image for how clear intentions get muddied by the world.
misreadings: Not a judgement on people with little money; the fault is the swagger, not the amount.
speaks_to: feeling one's ideals get muddied by daily life
not_for: someone ashamed of their modest means

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 16, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 17: off by one.
translation_note: Fine. Note Swami Prajnananand's alternative reading in Manas Piyush (greed dries contentment); the common reading is ours.
context: The rains are over. Ram tells Lakshman how beautiful autumn is, again pairing each sight with a moral. These lines come right after the kasa grass flowering like old age.

key_terms.sense: the star Canopus, named after the sage Agastya, whose rising marks the end of the rains

core_teaching: Contentment dries up greed as the autumn star dries the puddles on the roads. A heart without pride and delusion is clear like autumn lakes.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Only the road water is said to dry completely; so contentment ends greed entirely. Road water is always dirty and keeps people off the road, as greed keeps people away from the greedy man.
Offers a second reading: greed dries up contentment. Until firm devotion comes, a little greed can destroy contentment, as with Sugriva, whose knowledge gave way to sense-greed through bad company.
Rivers are like saints who wander and help many; lakes like saints who stay in one place. Autumn clearing the water is like a guru clearing the heart.
Renders it as the rising of Canopus drying the roads as greed is dried up by contentment.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for wanting less: contentment is not lack of ambition but the end of a restless craving, and with it the mind clears like water after rain.
misreadings: Not a call to give up all goals or accept injustice in the name of contentment.
speaks_to: seeking a clear mind after a turbulent period
not_for: someone in real material need, for whom 'be content' sounds dismissive

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 16, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 17: off by one.
context: In Ram's autumn description, these lines come after the wagtails returning like good deeds in season. They are followed by the clear sky likened to a devotee who has given up all other hopes.

key_terms.sense: an unwise householder (with a family to support)

core_teaching: An earth with neither mud nor dust is like the rule of a wise king. Fish panic as the water shrinks, like an unwise family man when his money runs out: the wise plan and work, the unwise only panic.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: 'Abudh' means one without the skill or learning to earn more; a capable person with a large family does not panic but works to support them. The ruler should be neither too hot nor too cold, but act by policy.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank, quoted in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Builds a detailed parallel: many fish and little water like a big family and little money; clouds gone like income stopped; the fish cannot leave the water as the householder cannot leave home.
All old manuscripts read 'abudh'; some modern editors print 'bibidh'. Compares Bhagavata 10.20.38 on creatures in shallow water and the miserly poor householder.
Renders it as fish distressed like improvident men of family at the loss of money.

practical_reading: Used as a nudge to prepare for lean seasons, and to respond to money trouble with planning rather than panic.
misreadings: Not a judgement on anyone who is poor or struggling.
Not a claim that worry about money is foolish; the contrast is between panic and wise effort.
cautions: 'Unwise' (abudh) carries a judgement; a reader in financial distress may feel blamed. Keep the focus on planning, not fault.
not_for: someone who has just lost a job or is in debt crisis
someone already ashamed about money

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 20, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 21: off by one. The text reads बिषय (our data has विषय, a spelling variant).
translation_note: Fine. Second line is narration: Lakshman, pleased, reassured him.
context: Settled into kingship, Sugriva forgets his promise to search for Sita. Ram, angry, sends Lakshman; Hanuman and Tara intervene. Sugriva comes out, falls at Lakshman's feet and confesses. After this, Hanuman reports the search parties already sent and they go to Ram.

key_terms.sense: the objects of the senses, sensual pleasures

core_teaching: No intoxicant is like sense-pleasure: it can cloud even a sage's mind in a moment. Owning one's lapse humbly brings forgiveness.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Other intoxicants bewilder the ignorant; sense-pleasure bewilders even the wise. Calling Lakshman 'Nath' means: you made me protected once by killing Bali, and now by your grace I am protected again after the senses nearly undid me.
In Valmiki 4.35 Tara makes the same plea, citing Vishvamitra, who spent ten years with the nymph Ghritachi and thought it a day.
There Lakshman says his harsh words came from loving anger and asks Sugriva to forgive them; Vijayanand Tripathi expands Lakshman's reassurance.

practical_reading: Used for owning up when comfort or distraction has made us forget a commitment: name the lapse, apologise without excuses, and get back to the task.
misreadings: Not an excuse ('even sages fall, so it's fine'); Sugriva uses it to confess, not to justify.
cautions: Could feed shame in someone struggling with addiction; pair with the forgiveness that follows.
speaks_to: having let someone down through distraction or comfort
not_for: someone in active addiction crisis who needs practical help, not a proverb

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 28, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 29: off by one.
context: The search party, despairing on the southern shore, has spoken of Jatayu's death. His elder brother, the vulture Sampati, hears it, performs his brother's rites, and tells his story: as young birds the two flew toward the sun. He then tells of the sage Chandrama, who foretold that he would help Ram's messengers.

key_terms.sense: could not bear the sun's heat

core_teaching: Sampati's own account: his brother turned back, but he in his pride flew on and was burned and fell. Pride is named as the cause of the fall.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: If he had turned back too, the brothers' strength would have been counted equal; he thought himself stronger, so he went on. The fruit of pride is suffering, and he got it.
Sampati tells this story to raise the monkeys' spirits, then tells the sage's prophecy to show he can point them to Sita.
Compares Adhyatma Ramayana, where the brothers, proud of their strength, flew toward the sun to test it. Adds that by grace his body was not shattered, since it was needed for Ram's work later.

practical_reading: Used as a cautionary tale about overreaching to prove oneself, and about the honesty of naming one's own pride.
misreadings: Not a lesson against ambition as such; the fault named is proud rivalry.
speaks_to: learning from a fall caused by overconfidence
not_for: someone injured or disabled, who may hear it as 'you brought it on yourself'

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 29, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 30: off by one.
context: Sampati has told the monkeys that Lanka lies a hundred yojanas across the sea and that he can see Sita there. As he speaks, his burned wings grow back. He tells them whoever can cross the sea will do Ram's work, and urges courage. Then he leaves, and the monkeys debate who can leap.
core_teaching: Only one with both strength and wisdom can do this task. Sampati's own renewed body is visible proof of what grace can do, so the monkeys should take heart.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: First Sampati told them all to do the Lord's work; now he says one of them must, the one who can leap the sea, and names who is fit. 'Look at me' shows that his wings regrew as he spoke.
It is Ram's work: Ram himself will help and give the wit, so do not panic, just be ready to act.
In Valmiki 4.63 Sampati's wings sprout before the monkeys, and he says this is a sign that they will succeed.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to discouragement: look at concrete examples of recovery, including your own, before deciding a task is impossible.
misreadings: Not a promise that a hard task will be easy; it calls for both strength and intelligence.
speaks_to: a team that has lost heart
not_for: someone whose recovery has not come, who may feel the comparison as pressure

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 29, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id and label say 4.30: off by one.
context: Right after showing his regrown wings, Sampati gives the monkeys a second argument for courage before he leaves. The monkeys then each state how far they can leap.
core_teaching: If even sinners cross the endless ocean of existence by remembering Ram's name, his own messengers can surely cross a hundred-yojana sea. Drop the fear, keep Ram in mind, and find a way.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: After giving visible proof (his own body), Sampati gives scriptural proof. If sinners can cross the endless ocean of existence, what is a hundred yojanas to you?
Quotes the Adhyatma Ramayana parallel: those who remember Vishnu cross the ocean of samsara, so Ram's dear devotees can surely cross a mere sea.
Cites Tulsi's Hanuman Bahuk, where the monkeys are 'beaten' after looking at the ocean: their joy had gone and their courage failed.

practical_reading: Used to turn fear into planning: hold on to what you trust, then 'make the effort' (karahu upai). Faith here is a reason to act, not to wait.
misreadings: Not a promise that faith removes the need for a plan; the verse ends with 'find a way'.
cautions: Calls fear 'cowardice'; a reader with anxiety may feel judged.
not_for: clinical anxiety or panic, where 'drop your fear' is not helpful on its own
research_note: prasang is null in our data; it belongs with the Sampati episode (rcm.p for Sampati's burned wings).

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 30, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 31, which does not exist: Kishkindha Kand has 30 dohas.
translation_note: Fine. The quotation marks close after the first line; the second line is narration.
context: The monkeys have each said how far they can leap; none can cross. Old Jambavant, king of the bears, turns to Hanuman, who has been sitting silent, and reminds him he is the wind's son, a treasury of wisdom. These lines are the climax; Hanuman then grows huge and asks what he should do. Sundar Kand follows.

key_terms.sense: you were born for Ram's work

core_teaching: Being reminded of one's purpose restores forgotten strength. Hanuman grows the moment he hears that his life is for Ram's work.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Jambavant speaks because he is the eldest and king of the bears, so only he could rouse Hanuman. He asks why the strong one sits silent while all others declare their strength.
Hanuman stayed silent so as not to take the honour of being Ram's envoy from anyone who wanted it; Jambavant understood and asked him to speak.
The silence was Ram's prompting: had Hanuman volunteered first, others could say they could have done it. A true worker does not insist that only he will do the job.
Valmiki's Uttara Kanda tells of a curse that makes Hanuman forget his strength until reminded; Adhyatma Ramayana has Jambavant say Hanuman was born for Ram's work.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for self-doubt: sometimes we need someone to remind us what we are capable of and what we are here for, and we can be that voice for others.
misreadings: Not a claim that anyone can do anything; it is about a specific gift and purpose being recalled.
not_for: someone told 'you can do anything' while facing real limits, e.g. illness

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 1 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Reference matches.
translation_note: Fine. The speech line is Hanuman's; the first half is narration.
context: Hanuman has just leapt from the shore toward Lanka. The ocean, seeing he is Ram's envoy, tells the mountain Mainaka to rise and give him a rest. Hanuman touches it, bows and flies on. Next the gods send Surasa to test him.

key_terms.sense: touched with his hand (an honour to the mountain)
a bow of respect and leave-taking

core_teaching: Hanuman honours the kind offer but will not rest before the task is done. Courtesy toward helpers and single-minded commitment go together.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Mainaka took human form and offered rest (as in Valmiki 5.1). Hanuman honoured it with a touch, and bowed because Mainaka is a god and his father's friend. The bow is also a farewell.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki and Ananda Ramayana)
commentaries.gist: In Valmiki Hanuman says he is pleased with the hospitality but has vowed not to stop on the way, and touches the mountain. In Ananda Ramayana Mainaka asks to be purified by his touch.
The poet compresses the whole exchange into one doha to show Hanuman's speed: he is half-way across while Mainaka is still being told to rise.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to focus: acknowledge and thank those who offer comfort, but finish what matters before you rest.
misreadings: Not a rule against rest or self-care; it is about not stopping mid-task when something urgent depends on you.
Not a model for refusing all help.
cautions: Could feed burnout or guilt about resting in someone already overworking.
speaks_to: staying focused on an important commitment
distractions on the way to a goal
not_for: someone exhausted or burnt out who needs permission to stop

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand, opening Sanskrit shloka 2 (mangalacharan), before doha 1. Reference matches.
attribution_note: Speaker is Tulsidas in his own invocation; fine.
context: Each kand of the Manas opens with Sanskrit invocation verses. This is the second of three at the start of Sundar Kand, between a praise of Ram and the famous verse to Hanuman. It is often recited on its own.

key_terms.sense: the inner self of all, who knows every heart
full, overflowing devotion; or devotion that hands over all one's burden
desire and the other faults (anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy)

core_teaching: A prayer from someone who wants nothing but devotion: since Ram knows every heart, the claim can be checked. It asks for two things: full devotion, and a mind kept clean of desire and the other inner enemies.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: 'No other longing' means not wanting powers, wealth, dharma, pleasure or even liberation. Desire is named first because it is the chief obstacle to devotion.
'Nirbhara' has two senses: full and unwavering, and the devotion in which one hands over the whole burden of life to Ram and is free of care. Both apply.
The second line asks for both gaining (devotion) and keeping (protection from desire and the rest), since even a devotee's clear mind can be muddied, as Narada's was.

practical_reading: Recited daily as a centring prayer: say honestly what you want most, and ask for help keeping the mind free of what pulls it away.
misreadings: Not a claim that the speaker has no desires at all; it asks for help with them.
speaks_to: wanting a simpler, more focused inner life
not_for: readers who are not religious, unless framed as an intention
research_note: prasang is null; it is a mangalacharan verse, not part of a story.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 2, chaupai lines 9-10 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Reference matches.
context: The gods send Surasa, mother of serpents, to test Hanuman's strength and wit. She blocks his path and says she will eat him. He asks to go first and return after his work; she refuses. Next he slips in and out of her mouth, bows and asks leave, and she blesses him.
core_teaching: Hanuman meets force with force, but when force cannot win he becomes tiny and passes through. Knowing when to grow and when to shrink is the wisdom the gods wanted to test.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Surasa grew her mouth without pattern; Hanuman always showed exactly double, only to show her, not to harm her. When she reached her limit he went to the limit of smallness.
This is a test of divine powers; both show their siddhi of greatness. 'As ... so' covers the three rounds of the contest.
Her mouth reaching a hundred yojanas, the width of the sea, filled his whole path; the smallest form is the answer to the largest threat.

practical_reading: Used to teach flexibility: some obstacles are overcome by matching strength, others by humility and quick wit.
misreadings: Not a lesson in shrinking oneself to avoid all conflict; it is about choosing the right response.
speaks_to: facing an obstacle that keeps growing
negotiation and knowing when to yield

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 3: off by one.
context: Entering Lanka at night in a tiny form, Hanuman is stopped by Lankini, guardian of the city. He knocks her down with a blow. She recalls Brahma's sign that when a monkey strikes her the demons' end is near, and counts herself lucky to have seen Ram's messenger. This doha is her praise of good company. She then blesses him to enter.

key_terms.sense: a tiny fraction of time, an instant

core_teaching: Put the joys of heaven and of liberation together on one pan of a scale: they still do not weigh as much as one moment in the company of a saint.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: The scale is the intellect. Heaven stands for ritual action, liberation for knowledge, and satsang for devotion; satsang is both the first step of devotion and its fruit, so it outweighs both.
The same idea is in Bhagavata 1.18.13, where the sages say they would not weigh heaven or liberation against a moment's company with those devoted to God.
The scale image makes it visible: the pan with heaven rises, the pan with satsang stays on the ground because it is heavier.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to value time with good people: a short conversation with someone wise and kind can do more than great achievements.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of other goals; it ranks them by what lasts.
speaks_to: finding a mentor or spiritual community
feeling that good company has changed you
not_for: someone isolated without access to such company, who may feel the lack sharply

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 5, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 4: off by one.
attribution_note: Line 1 is Lankini. In Manas Piyush the second line runs into the next (the one on whom Ram looks with grace) and is read as Kakbhushundi's narratorial aside to Garuda, not Lankini's words.
translation_note: 'For such a one' is right in sense, but the condition (Ram's gracious look) is in the next line, which our text omits. Consider adding it.
context: Lankini, humbled, blesses Hanuman and sends him into Lanka. The second line continues into the third: all this happens to the one on whom Ram has looked with grace. Hanuman then enters the city in a tiny form.

key_terms.sense: the ocean becomes a cow's hoofprint

core_teaching: Go about your work holding Ram in your heart. For one on whom Ram looks with grace, obstacles turn into help: poison into nectar, enemies into friends, the sea into a puddle, fire into coolness.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Lankini tells him to enter fearlessly; 'all the work' means more than finding Sita. Every item came true for Hanuman: Surasa's threat became a blessing, Lankini an ally, the sea a hoofprint, and later fire did not burn him.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (reading of line 2)
commentaries.gist: Lines 2-3 belong together and are addressed to Garuda (reading गरुड as a vocative): this is Kakbhushundi's comment as narrator, not Lankini's. Kodavram's text reads गरुअ (heavy) instead.
Contrasts Aranya Kand, where for one turned away from Ram, nectar becomes poison and a friend acts like a hundred enemies.

practical_reading: Used before a hard task: keep in mind whom or what you serve, and difficulties can turn into help along the way.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that faith makes all danger vanish; Hanuman still acts with skill and courage.
cautions: Promises can sound like 'nothing bad will happen'; avoid with readers facing real danger.
speaks_to: starting a daunting job or move
not_for: someone in danger who needs practical safety steps
someone whose prayers seem unanswered

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 6: off by one.
context: Searching Lanka, Hanuman finds a house marked with Ram's name and meets Vibhishan, Ravana's brother. After they exchange who they are, Vibhishan describes his life among the demons and wonders whether Ram will ever be kind to him. Then he answers himself here. Hanuman replies by telling of his own lowliness.

key_terms.sense: a body of tamas, a demon's birth
without God's grace one does not meet the good

core_teaching: Vibhishan feels he has no birth, practice or love that qualifies him. Yet meeting a true devotee is itself the sign of grace, so he now has hope.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: He declares himself without knowledge (tamas body), action (no practice) and devotion (no love for the feet). He answers his own question because the answer would not sound right from Hanuman's mouth. Hanuman is his doorway to Ram.
Reads 'tamas body' as lack of action and 'no practice' as lack of knowledge.
Hearing Hanuman's story, Vibhishan knows he is Ram's envoy and that his own good can come through him, so he speaks of his helplessness.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to feeling unworthy: the arrival of a good person or a helping hand can itself be a sign you have not been forgotten.
misreadings: Not a claim that birth decides worth.
cautions: Self-description as low by birth can echo caste or self-contempt; keep the emphasis on hope.
not_for: someone with severe low self-worth who may latch onto the first line

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 7 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 6: off by one.
context: Just after Vibhishan's hope, Hanuman tells him: 'What lineage do I have? A fickle monkey, low in every way; say my name in the morning and you go without food that day.' This doha completes that thought. After it, the narrator says those who forget such a master suffer, and Hanuman finds peace in telling Ram's virtues.
core_teaching: Hanuman offers his own life as evidence: if Ram was kind to someone as lowly as him, Vibhishan need not doubt. Remembering that kindness moves him to tears.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Hanuman recalls one virtue in particular, Ram's lifting of the lowly, so the singular 'gun' is used. By calling himself lower than Vibhishan, he confirms that grace will surely come to Vibhishan.
'Sakha' marks three likenesses: both share a tamasic nature, both lived under a powerful brother (Bali, Ravana), and the same Ram who helped one will help the other.
If Ram was kind to me, how much more to those rich in dharma, and to you, a great devotee.

practical_reading: Used for encouraging someone through one's own story: 'if it happened for me, it can happen for you'.
misreadings: Hanuman's self-description is humility, not a teaching that anyone is truly worthless.
speaks_to: encouraging a friend who feels unworthy
not_for: someone who needs their worth affirmed rather than a shared self-lowering

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 14, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 12: off by two.
context: Hanuman has dropped Ram's ring before Sita in the Ashok grove, told Ram's story and identified himself as Ram's messenger. Sita, convinced, is moved. After this she asks after Ram and Lakshman and whether Ram remembers her.

key_terms.sense: the Lord's own person, his servant
love grew very deep (variant: बाढ़ी, grew greatly)

core_teaching: Sita, drowning in the sea of separation, finds in Hanuman a ship. Knowing he belongs to Ram, her love for him overflows.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Seeing a devotee makes love rise by itself. Her love had begun when he told Ram's story, held back by doubt; now, sure, it overflowed in tears and thrill.
Valmiki 5.34-35: Sita says love for him arose in her mind on seeing him, and she sheds tears of joy on knowing him as Ram's envoy.
Several manuscripts read बाढ़ी (grew); Bhagavatdas's reads गाढ़ी (deep). Our text uses गाढ़ी.

practical_reading: Used for the moment help arrives in isolation: one messenger, call or friend can be the boat in a sea of loneliness.
misreadings: Not a suggestion that one person can or should carry all of someone's loneliness.
speaks_to: loneliness or separation from a loved one
the relief of a message from someone far away

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 14, chaupai lines 9-10 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 12: off by two.
context: Sita has asked whether Ram ever remembers her and cried that he has forgotten her completely; she is near collapse. Hanuman answers gently. After this he gives Ram's own message about his love.
core_teaching: Sita fears she has been forgotten. Hanuman tells her the opposite: Ram suffers with her, and his love for her is twice hers for him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: This answers her cry that Ram had forgotten her, just as Ram told Hanuman not to feel slighted when Hanuman thought he had been forgotten: 'you are twice as dear as Lakshman'.
'Mother' opens the line because Hanuman, seeing her state, is himself overcome and can only say 'mother' before going on.
In Gitavali Hanuman asks why she speaks so pitifully: Ram's body has grown thin but his heart has grown full of love.

practical_reading: Used for anyone who feels forgotten by someone they love who is far away: the absence may hide a love as great as theirs.
misreadings: Not a promise that every absent person secretly loves you more.
cautions: Could comfort someone falsely about an estranged or abusive partner; frame it as about Ram, not about every relationship.
not_for: someone who has actually been abandoned or rejected

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 15, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 13: off by two.
attribution_note: Line 7 is Ram's message as delivered by Hanuman; line 8 is narration.
translation_note: Fine.
context: Hanuman delivers Ram's message to Sita: since parting, everything has turned against him; the moon burns like the sun, the cool breeze like a serpent's breath; only his mind knows the truth of their love. This verse ends the message. Then Sita is lost in love and Hanuman urges her to take heart.
core_teaching: The essence of Ram's love is simply this: his mind is always with her. Hearing it, Sita forgets herself in love.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Answers her question whether Ram ever remembers her: his mind lives with her always. Ram suffers in body, says little in words, and his mind stays with her: that is the whole message.
The constant, undistracted dwelling of the mind on the beloved is the key to 'priti-ras'; lover and beloved appear as two bodies but are one.
'Vaidehi' (bodiless) is chosen because she forgets her body on hearing it.

practical_reading: Used to express love across distance: what matters is where the heart stays, not physical presence.
misreadings: Not an argument that physical presence does not matter.
speaks_to: separation from a spouse or partner
not_for: someone grieving a death, where 'my mind is always with you' may land differently

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 15, chaupai lines 9-10 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 13: off by two.
context: Sita is lost in love after hearing Ram's message. Hanuman steadies her. He goes on to say Ram's arrows will burn the demons like cotton, and that Ram would have come already had he known where she was.

key_terms.sense: giver of joy to his servants

core_teaching: In hardship, steadiness comes first. Recall the one you trust and what he can do, and let fear go.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Patience in calamity is the main thing, so Hanuman tells her four times to hold steady: to hear the message, to remember Ram, for the demons' death, and for Ram's coming.
Hanuman uses 'mata' when she is overwhelmed and 'janani' when she is composed; the tender word is chosen to bring her back.

practical_reading: Used as a steadying word for someone frightened: breathe, recall what you can rely on, then face the fear.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of fear as weakness.
cautions: 'Give up faint-heartedness' can sound like blame to someone with anxiety.
speaks_to: fear while waiting for rescue or news
not_for: clinical anxiety where 'stop being afraid' is unhelpful

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 16 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 14: off by two.
context: Sita doubts that small monkeys can beat Ravana's mighty demons. Hanuman shows his huge golden form, then becomes small again and says this. Sita is reassured and blesses him.

key_terms.sense: Garuda, the eagle, eater of snakes

core_teaching: Hanuman credits nothing to himself: monkeys have no special strength or wit, but with the Lord's power behind them the smallest can overcome the greatest.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: The huge form and the wise words he just showed are not monkey qualities; they are Ram's power. Ram's power can make the tiny snake eat Garuda, as the monkeys, demons' food, will eat the demons.
Cites a Puranic tale of a snake that took refuge in Vishnu and was empowered to turn on Garuda.
Compares Hanuman's later answer to Ram (doha 33): by your power, cotton can burn the submarine fire.

practical_reading: Used against feeling outmatched: what you lack in size or skill, the strength of your cause and those behind you can supply.
misreadings: Not a denial of one's own effort or ability.
speaks_to: feeling small against a powerful opponent
a small team taking on a big task

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 22 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 20: off by two.
context: Hanuman, bound by Meghnad's Brahma-weapon, stands before Ravana. He has told Ravana who he is and why he fought. Now he counsels him: give up enmity, return Sita, and take refuge. After this he urges Ravana to rule Lanka with Ram in his heart and not stain Pulastya's line. Ravana mocks him and orders his tail burned.

key_terms.sense: enemy of Khara (and so, for the hostile, a destroyer)

core_teaching: Even to his captor, Hanuman holds the door open: Ram protects whoever bows, and if Ravana seeks refuge, his offence will be forgotten.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Three epithets: he protects the humble (rajas), is compassionate (sattva), and kills the wicked like Khara (tamas). Ravana's offence is not forgivable, yet the Lord forgets it entirely.
'Pranat' shows even a bow is enough; 'Kharari' reminds Ravana that only God could have killed Khara, so there is no shame in surrender, and that the alternative is death.

practical_reading: Used to say that it is never too late to turn around: even after great wrong, an honest turn can be met with mercy.
misreadings: Not a claim that consequences vanish; Ravana's offence is forgiven only if he turns, and he does not.
Not a teaching that victims must forgive.
cautions: Ravana refuses; the story continues to his death.
speaks_to: feeling it is too late to change
not_for: someone harmed by another, who may hear it as pressure to forgive the harmer

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 23, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 21: off by two.
translation_note: Fine. 'Slip away even while held, and having them is like not having them' is one attested reading of a famously knotty half-line; Manas Piyush lists several others.
context: Continuing his counsel to Ravana in court, Hanuman has just said that speech without Ram's name has no beauty, like a fully ornamented woman without clothes. This verse follows. Next he says a man who turns from Ram finds no protection anywhere.

key_terms.sense: goes even while it stays; had and as good as not had
a source fed by water, a spring

core_teaching: Wealth and power without a deeper root are like rivers fed only by rain: they swell for a season and then dry up.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Reads the half-line in time: what one had, has and will get is all wasted. Or: what one has will go and be as if never had, like a rain-river that dries up as if water never flowed.
What remains goes; what has been got is as good as not got. For the one turned from Ram, wealth is no means to the highest good.
Lists several further readings and calls some 'mere wordplay'. Notes that wealth is Lakshmi's grace; it shines only when used for the Lord's work and good deeds.

practical_reading: Used to ask what one's success is rooted in: achievements without values or purpose behind them do not last or satisfy.
misreadings: Not a claim that the wealthy are bad or that money is evil.
not_for: someone in poverty, where a sermon on wealth can sound beside the point

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 27, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 25: off by two.
context: After burning Lanka, Hanuman returns to Sita and asks for a token. She gives her hair-jewel (chudamani) and this message for Ram. Next she asks him to remind Ram of the crow incident and to come within a month, or she will not live.

key_terms.sense: one whose every wish is fulfilled, who needs nothing
a pledged name, a reputation one is bound to honour

core_teaching: Sita appeals not to Ram's need of her (he needs nothing) but to his pledged nature: he is known as the friend of the helpless, so let him honour that and end her trouble.

commentaries.who: Panjabiji and Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Thus' suggests she showed the gesture of bowing, hands joined, so Hanuman could convey it exactly. 'You lack nothing' means: you value the feeling behind the offering.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: You gain nothing from me, but recall your pledged name. You are able; it is not right that I suffer while you have the power. 'My' goes with both 'lord' and 'trouble'.

practical_reading: Used as a model of prayer or appeal in crisis: humble, direct, and resting on the known kindness of the one asked.
misreadings: Not a substitute for asking concrete help from people around you.
cautions: Part of a message that ends with a threat to her life if Ram is late; keep it separate in fragile contexts.
speaks_to: praying or asking for help in a crisis
sending a message to someone far away
not_for: someone expecting prayer alone to solve an emergency

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 30 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 28: off by two.
translation_note: Fine. Our text reads दिवस निसि; Manas Piyush notes many manuscripts read रात दिनु and chose दिवस निसि.
context: Hanuman has returned to Ram. Ram asks how Sita is and how she keeps herself alive. Hanuman says her eyes are full, her mind absorbed in Ram's feet, and gives this image. After it he delivers her message and the jewel.

key_terms.sense: eyes locked on her own feet (head bowed)
by what path could life leave

core_teaching: Sita lives because she guards herself: Ram's name stands watch day and night, remembering him is the closed door, and her lowered eyes are the lock. Life has no way out.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: She sits day and night head bowed, absorbed in meditation, constantly saying the name: with doors shut and chained and guards on watch, how could anyone leave?
In Valmiki 5, Sita says she thinks of Ram constantly and says his name, so she sees and hears only him.
Compares Gitavali 5.18-19, where Hanuman describes her eyes still as a painting and her tongue repeating the name, and Kausalya's similar lament in Gitavali 2.53.

practical_reading: Used for how remembrance and routine can hold a person together through a long ordeal.
misreadings: Not a claim that devotion replaces help or rescue; Ram goes to rescue her.
cautions: Concerns whether someone will die; a reader with suicidal thoughts needs direct support, not only this image.
speaks_to: holding on during captivity, illness or separation
not_for: someone in acute crisis or with suicidal thoughts, without added support

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 32, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 30: off by two.
context: Hanuman has told Ram how Sita lives and given her message. Ram weeps. He asks how one who relies on him could meet such calamity. Hanuman answers in the next verse.
core_teaching: God, the home of joy, weeps at his devotee's pain, and asks how one who depends on him wholly could be in such trouble.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: The Almighty grieved as if helpless; joy itself grieves at a devotee's pain. One devoted to Ram should not meet calamity: in waking there is none, in sleep nothing is known, and in dream one sees what one dwells on.
'Home of joy' fits: had Sita been happy without him he would have grieved; hearing her love, he is happy, and the tears are of feeling.
Lists several readings of 'bujhia' (should one ask / could one know calamity even in a dream) from Ramkumar, Deenji and Shrikant Sharan; concludes it means 'should'.

practical_reading: Used to show that the divine is moved by human suffering, and that a devotee's pain is never unseen.
misreadings: Not a promise that devotees never suffer; the next verse redefines what real calamity is.
cautions: Can imply that suffering means lack of faith; pair with the next verse and avoid for those in acute hardship.
not_for: someone whose suffering is ongoing and who may hear 'true devotees don't suffer'

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 32, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 30: off by two.
context: Ram has asked whether one wholly devoted to him could meet calamity. Hanuman answers, then assures him the demons are nothing to him. Ram then tells Hanuman he cannot repay him.
core_teaching: The only real calamity is losing the remembrance of God. Outward trouble, like the demons, can be overcome.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Sita remembers with mind and speech; what she lacks is serving Ram in body, and that is her calamity. The demons stand in the way, so killing them ends it.
Hanuman both affirms and resolves: remembrance is present, so there is no calamity; service is absent, and that will be fixed by victory.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to reframe hardship: outward trouble can be faced; the deeper loss is losing touch with what gives life meaning. Then act: Hanuman immediately turns to the plan.
misreadings: Not a denial that outward suffering is real; Hanuman still commits to rescuing Sita.
Not 'just pray and it will go away'.
cautions: Can minimise real suffering if quoted alone.
not_for: someone in acute suffering who needs it acknowledged first

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 33, chaupai line 9 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 31: off by two. A single line (two charans), the last before the doha.
attribution_note: prasang in our data is 'Hanuman speaks plainly to Ravana', but this verse is spoken to Ram after Hanuman's return. Wrong prasang.
translation_note: Fine.
context: Ram asks how Hanuman burned Ravana's fortress. Hanuman, pleased and humble, says a monkey's only bravery is jumping from branch to branch; crossing the sea, burning the golden city, killing demons and wrecking the grove were all Ram's doing. The doha follows: nothing is beyond one whom Ram favours.
core_teaching: Hanuman gives all credit for his feats to Ram's power.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: He confines his own effort to branch-jumping and credits the rest to Ram. He even lists the deeds out of order, burning first, which shows lack of pride (or simply answers Ram's question first).

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Hanuman Nataka and Kavitavali)
commentaries.gist: Hanuman Nataka says the sea was crossed by Ram's power and Lanka already burned by Sita's sighs and Ram's anger, the monkey only an occasion; Kavitavali 5.22 says the same.
Ram's ring carried him over, Sita's jewel brought him back, and Lanka burned from her grief and Ram's glory.

practical_reading: Used to model humility about success: give credit to the team, mentors or grace behind an achievement.
misreadings: Not a denial of one's own effort or a reason to refuse praise for real work.
cautions: For someone with low self-worth, may reinforce discounting their own achievements.
not_for: someone who habitually belittles their own achievements

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 34, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 32: off by two.
attribution_note: Line 1 is Hanuman; line 2 is Shiva narrating to Bhavani (Parvati).
translation_note: Fine.
context: Ram has told Hanuman that no god, man or sage has helped him like this and he cannot repay him. Hanuman falls at his feet. Asked to name a gift, he asks only for devotion. Shiva, narrating to Parvati, then says whoever knows Ram's nature cannot care for anything but worship.
core_teaching: Offered any reward, Hanuman asks only for unwavering devotion, and Ram grants it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Other good things give joy; devotion gives the highest joy. He asks now because Ram is pleased, and because a servant should not be 'repaid' as an equal; devotion keeps the Lord favourable always.
'Ati sukh' is the joy beyond the senses that the Gita (6.21) calls grasped by the intellect alone.

practical_reading: Used to ask what we really want when offered a reward: steady love for what matters rather than another prize.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all other goods.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 37 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 35: off by two. Dohavali 524 has the same doha with the order 'mantri, guru, vaid'.
translation_note: Fine. Read crosswise: minister to kingdom, doctor to body, teacher to dharma (Manas Piyush calls it a deliberate broken order).
context: Ram's army has reached the shore. In Lanka, Mandodari pleads with Ravana; he laughs. His ministers flatter him that the monkeys are nothing. Tulsidas comments with this doha, then says this was exactly Ravana's case: his court sang his praise.

key_terms.sense: speak pleasing words out of fear or hope of reward

core_teaching: When advisers, doctors and teachers say only what pleases, out of fear or hope of reward, the kingdom, the body and righteousness are soon ruined.

commentaries.gist: A Hitopadesha verse says the king whose doctor, guru and minister speak only pleasantly soon loses body, dharma and treasury. A doctor who gives the patient what he craves kills him; a guru who does not stop wrongdoing destroys both.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: The order here is deliberately crossed: Ravana's minister flatters, his doctor Sushen later saves Lakshman, and his 'guru' Shiva never stopped him from opposing Ram.

practical_reading: Widely quoted for workplaces and families: seek and value people who tell you the truth, and be that person for others.
misreadings: Not licence for harshness; the fault is flattery from fear or self-interest, not kindness.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 38, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 36: off by two.
context: Vibhishan enters Ravana's court and, invited to speak, gives sober advice: for welfare, fame and good fortune, give up looking at another's wife; then these lines. The doha that follows tells Ravana to drop desire, anger, pride and greed, the roads to hell, and worship Ram.

key_terms.sense: sole lord of all fourteen worlds
an ocean of virtues and refined

core_teaching: No power is safe if it is used to harm living beings, and even a little greed spoils the name of an otherwise good person.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Lord of fourteen worlds means all power; 'cannot stand' means it loses the power to protect itself, and merit and self are soon destroyed.
Rule kept by the sword and law alone, without keeping the people content, soon falls; the line also hints at the governments of the poet's own time.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Harming beings is opposing God, who is in all beings. Desire and anger subside, but greed never does, so a little greed outweighs an ocean of virtue.

practical_reading: Used in leadership and ethics: power that harms people does not last, and small greed can undo a good reputation.
misreadings: Not a claim that any self-interest is sinful.
speaks_to: temptation to cut corners for gain

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 40, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 38: off by two.
context: Ravana has thrown out his old minister Malyavan for giving the same advice. Vibhishan, joining his palms, says this, then tells Ravana that bad sense has taken over his heart so he takes friend for foe, and loves Sita, the dark night of the demon race.

key_terms.sense: calamity, and ruin in the end

core_teaching: Both wisdom and folly live in every heart. Which one leads decides whether prosperity or ruin follows.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ravana had called Vibhishan and Malyavan fools; Vibhishan replies that sense is not decided by calling names but by its fruits. 'Nidana' means calamity and then ruin.
Good sense is sattvic understanding; bad sense is rajasic, which cannot tell right from wrong (Gita 18.31).
Cites a Sanskrit subhashita that good and bad sense are the two causes of all fortune and misfortune, and Kaikeyi's 'kumati' as an example of calamity.

practical_reading: Used to remind us that everyone carries both impulses; the work is noticing which one is steering a decision.
misreadings: Not a way to label people as simply good-minded or bad-minded.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 41, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 39: off by two.
attribution_note: Line 7 is Shiva's comment to Uma; line 8 is Vibhishan to Ravana. Our speaker field lists only Vibhishan; the translation marks both correctly.
translation_note: Fine.
context: Ravana, furious, calls Vibhishan a traitor living on his bread and kicks him. Vibhishan keeps clasping his feet. Shiva, narrating to Uma, comments (line 7); Vibhishan speaks (line 8). Then he leaves with his ministers by the sky road and goes to Ram.

key_terms.sense: this is the greatness of a saint
your good lies in worshipping Ram

core_teaching: A saint's greatness is to keep wishing well to the one who harms him. Vibhishan, kicked, still treats his brother as a father and tells him plainly where his good lies.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Vibhishan is the limit of goodness and Ravana of wickedness. Returning good for harm is praiseworthy only in a saint; in a warrior or king, kindness to an enemy is counted a fault, as Ram himself says.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Answers Ravana's 'you live by my keeping': you are like a father who raised me, so striking me was fine; a son's duty is to save his father, so I tell you to worship Ram.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki and Adhyatma)
commentaries.gist: Valmiki 6.16 and Adhyatma 6.2 both have Vibhishan call the elder brother 'like a father'.

practical_reading: Used for responding to hurt without hatred: you can keep goodwill and say the truth, and still walk away.
misreadings: Not a rule that one must accept being hit; Vibhishan leaves immediately after.
Commentary itself limits this to saints, not rulers or protectors.
cautions: Mentions physical violence by a family member; do not use to counsel someone to stay with an abuser.
not_for: someone experiencing domestic violence
someone pressured to keep 'being good' to an abuser

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 41 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 39: off by two.
context: Just kicked by Ravana, Vibhishan rises into the sky with his four ministers and says this so all can hear. The moment he leaves, the narrator says, the demons lost their life-force. He goes to Ram's camp full of hopes.

key_terms.sense: in the grip of death, of time

core_teaching: Vibhishan leaves openly, not in secret: Ram's will is true, this court is doomed, and he is going to Ram for refuge, so let no one call it betrayal.

commentaries.gist: Valmiki 6.17 names the four ministers who went with him (Anala, Panasa, Sampati, Pramati); they later spied on Ravana's camp for Ram, showing he came to serve.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Among the seven limbs of a kingdom the minister is chief; with ministers kept, what is lost can be rebuilt, which is why Vibhishan takes his with him.
He openly says he is going to Ram so that no one can later blame him for deserting or spying.

practical_reading: Used for leaving a harmful situation with honesty: say why you go, without hatred, and go towards something better.
misreadings: Not a justification for betraying a group for personal gain; the leaving is open and after honest counsel was rejected.
cautions: Raises family loyalty versus conscience; sensitive for those estranged from family.
speaks_to: leaving a toxic workplace or group
after being rejected for honest advice
not_for: someone who would read it as licence to cut off family impulsively

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 43, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 41: off by two.
attribution_note: Line 7 is Sugriva; line 8 is Ram. Our speaker field 'Sugriva / Ram' captures this.
translation_note: Fine.
context: Vibhishan arrives at Ram's camp. The guards tell Sugriva, who tells Ram. Ram asks his friend's view; Sugriva says demons are shape-shifters and this one has come to spy, so bind him (line 7). Ram answers (line 8). Hanuman is delighted. Ram then gives his refuge speech.

key_terms.sense: remover of the fear of whoever seeks refuge

core_teaching: Ram honours his friend's caution as good policy, but sets above it his vow to protect anyone who comes for refuge.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Sakha' implies Sugriva is eager to weigh the enemy and protect Ram's interests, which is a friend's duty.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ram refutes Sugriva gently, calling his view good so his friend is not hurt, then explains the duty to the refugee. Sugriva erred by jumping to faults without first praising Ram, as advisers properly do.
Valmiki 6.18.33: Ram's vow is to give fearlessness from all beings to anyone who comes once and says 'I am yours'.

practical_reading: Used to show how to overrule caution kindly: acknowledge the concern, then hold to a deeper principle.
misreadings: Not an argument against all caution or security; Ram addresses the risk directly next.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 44, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 42: off by two.
context: Ram has just said that those who abandon a refugee out of fear for themselves are sinners whose very sight is harmful. He continues to Sugriva with these lines, then explains why a truly wicked person would not come at all.

key_terms.sense: the killing of countless brahmins, the gravest sin

core_teaching: Ram does not turn away anyone who comes for refuge, whatever their past. The moment a soul truly turns towards him, the weight of countless lives of wrong is wiped away.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Those who abandon a refugee become wholly sinful, while even a great sinner who comes can be freed. Turning to God destroys sin; then worship becomes pleasing; worship purifies the mind; and the pure mind reaches God.
A sinner as such does not take refuge; the one who repents and then comes is not abandoned. Cites Gita 9.30-31: even the worst who worships single-mindedly is to be counted good.
One who sins deliberately, planning to take refuge later and be cleared, hopes in vain.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Reconciles this with Ram's earlier 'I do not like the enemy of brahmins': that was for people living by ordinary duties; this concerns full surrender.

practical_reading: Used to tell people that no past puts them beyond a fresh start, provided the turning is real.
misreadings: Not a licence to keep doing harm or to plan wrongdoing and 'repent later' (Ramshankar Sharan rules this out).
Does not cancel worldly consequences or the duty to repair harm.
cautions: Mentions killing; the hyperbole may need explaining for a general reader.
speaks_to: deep guilt or shame over the past
returning to faith after a long absence
not_for: someone harmed by another, if it is used to demand they accept the harmer back

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 44, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 42: off by two.
context: Continuing his answer to Sugriva's suspicion of Vibhishan: after saying he never abandons a refugee, Ram explains why Vibhishan's coming is itself evidence of his good heart. Next he says only the pure-minded reach him.
core_teaching: A wicked heart does not want to turn to God. That Vibhishan came to Ram at all shows his heart is not wicked.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Sin itself blocks worship, so the sinner never likes it. Ram would not reject even Ravana if he came, but a wicked heart will not come; Vibhishan's coming proves his purity. Cites Gita 7.15.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Ramanuja on Gita 7.15)
commentaries.gist: Draws on Ramanuja's bhashya on Gita 7.15, which describes four grades of those who do not take refuge: the deluded, the lowest, those whose knowledge is stolen by maya, and those of demonic disposition.

practical_reading: Used to encourage someone who doubts their own sincerity: the wish to turn toward the good is already a sign of a good heart.
misreadings: Not proof that anyone who shows up has pure motives in every case.
speaks_to: first steps back toward faith or recovery

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 44, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 42: off by two.
translation_note: 'Fault-finding' for छिद्र is loose. In this pairing (कपट छल छिद्र) it means looking for weak spots to exploit, i.e. scheming, which fits the spy context better.
context: Ram continues to answer Sugriva's suspicion. Having said the wicked would not come to him, he says what does reach him, then grants that even if Ravana sent Vibhishan as a spy, there is nothing to fear.

key_terms.sense: deceit, trickery and looking for weak spots

core_teaching: Only a clear, honest heart reaches God; he has no taste for deceit and scheming. And even if this were a spy, the camp has nothing to fear.

commentaries.gist: In Gitavali Ram calls Vibhishan wise, good, pure and a friend; Hanuman adds that a deceiver cannot face the Lord, as darkness cannot face the sun.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ram humours Sugriva: even granting he was sent, it is no fault of his, for his mind is clear; Ram knows Vibhishan's ways.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Even then' means even if our secrets are known; the repeated 'friend' shows Ram's affection for Sugriva while he overrules him.

practical_reading: Used to value transparency: honesty opens doors that cleverness cannot, and security that comes from strength need not fear the newcomer.
misreadings: Not a claim that suspicion is never justified.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 44, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 42: off by two.
context: Ram closes his answer to Sugriva. Then, in the doha, he tells Sugriva to bring Vibhishan either way, and the monkeys go to fetch him.

key_terms.sense: in the blink of an eye

core_teaching: There is no danger from a spy when Lakshman alone can destroy every demon in an instant. And if Vibhishan has come in fear for shelter, Ram will guard him like his own life.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ram shows divine power here but names Lakshman's, not his own; it is his way never to boast of his own prowess. Lakshman, as Shesha, incarnated to destroy demons.
Ram never states his own might; even in battle he names Lakshman and others.
In Valmiki 6.80 Lakshman offers to use the Brahma weapon to kill all demons, and Ram stops him from destroying many for one.

practical_reading: Used to show that real strength makes generosity possible: one who is secure can afford to protect the frightened.
misreadings: Not a boast of violence; the point is that there is nothing to fear from welcoming the frightened.
cautions: Mentions killing; keep the focus on protection.
speaks_to: fear of being taken advantage of

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 45 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 43: off by two. Ravana's sarcastic echo of the phrase 'श्रवन सुजसु सुनि' in doha 53 is a different doha.
translation_note: Fine. Manas Piyush prints आएउँ / सुजस (spelling variants).
context: Brought before Ram, Vibhishan is overwhelmed by his beauty. He says: Lord, I am Ravana's brother, born a demon, with a tamasic body that loves sin like an owl loves darkness. Then this plea. Ram embraces him at once.

key_terms.sense: the good fame heard with my ears
breaker of the fear of worldly existence
who gives joy to those who seek refuge

core_teaching: Vibhishan has come on the strength of Ram's reputation alone: he heard that Ram ends fear and distress, and asks to be saved.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Each epithet answers a lack in him: you are able, I am helpless; you end fear, I am afraid; you remove distress, I am distressed. His only claim is having heard that Ram protects any refugee.
Gitavali 5.43-44 expands the plea: he heard of the stone woman, the boatman, the vulture, Shabari and Sugriva, and comes as the enemy's brother insulted by his own kin.

practical_reading: Used for the moment of asking for help: you do not need credentials, only to come and ask.
misreadings: Not a formula that guarantees an outcome; it is a plea, and its force is in honesty.
speaks_to: asking for help after a crisis

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 46, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 44: off by two.
attribution_note: Manas Piyush (Pt. Ramkumar) reads line 7 ('better to live in hell...') as Ram speaking to Vibhishan, continuing Ram's questions about living among the wicked; Vibhishan's reply starts at line 8. Our data gives the whole verse to Vibhishan.
translation_note: The rendering is fine in wording, but if line 7 is Ram's, 'friend' (ताता) is Ram addressing Vibhishan; split the speakers.
context: Ram has embraced Vibhishan and asks after him: Lankesh, are you and your family well, living in a bad place among the wicked day and night? How do you keep your dharma? I know your ways; you are wise and dislike wrong. Then line 7; Vibhishan's reply begins in line 8. The doha says no soul knows peace until it worships Ram.
core_teaching: Better to live in hell than to be given the company of the wicked. And: having seen Ram's feet, Vibhishan is now truly well.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Reads line 7 as Ram's words: Ram himself states the harm of bad company, sparing Vibhishan from having to complain about his brother. Hell is preferred because it at least exhausts sin.
Quotes a Garuda Purana verse: better to live in hell than in a wicked house, since hell wears sin away while a bad house increases it.

commentaries.who: Nangeparamhans and Manas Tattva Bhaskar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: In hell one at least remembers God; in bad company never. Hell ends; bad company brings pain now and hell later.

practical_reading: Used to weigh company seriously: who we spend our days with shapes us more than our circumstances.
misreadings: Not contempt for people who live in hard places; it is about corrupting company.
Not a call to cut off everyone with faults.
cautions: Can sound harsh toward family members; Vibhishan's 'wicked company' is his own brother's court.
speaks_to: relief after escaping a toxic environment
not_for: someone who cannot leave their environment (a child, a dependant), who may feel condemned

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 47, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 45: off by two.
context: After Ram's teaching on what it means to be well, Vibhishan says all his fear and grief are gone through Ram's grace, then says this. The doha follows: how great is my fortune, that Ram's grace embraced me.

key_terms.sense: does not come even into sages' meditation

core_teaching: Vibhishan cannot believe his welcome: one who never did good has been embraced by the Lord whom sages cannot reach in meditation. Grace, not merit, did it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: He shows his lowness in body (a demon), mind (low nature) and action (no good deeds), as Shabari did. Even great merit cannot earn sight of the Lord; he comes by his own grace.
Here 'nishachar' is defined as one of low nature and 'adham' as one who does no good, as in Bal Kand 184.
Compares Gitavali 5.36: the form that sages and Shiva cannot see in dreams has taken Tulsi into its lap.

practical_reading: Used for undeserved welcome: the wonder of being accepted by someone far greater than you, without having earned it.
misreadings: The self-description is humility before grace, not a model for self-contempt.
cautions: Harsh self-judgement may echo shame for some readers.
not_for: someone with severe shame or self-hatred, without a reframe

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 48, chaupai lines 1-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 46. The text spans two chaupais and stops mid-sentence: line 4 (mother, father ... family) begins the list completed in the next verse.
translation_note: Two issues. (1) Manas Piyush reads line 3 as Ram setting aside the refugee's pride, delusion and deceit (overlooking them), not as the refugee giving them up first; our translation takes the second reading.
