Both are possible, but the editor should know. (2) The final line (जननी जनक ... परिवारा) is the start of the next sentence; our translation ends with a dangling colon. Either drop line 4 or merge with rcm.5.46.chaupai.3.
context: Vibhishan has rejoiced in Ram's grace. Ram now tells him his own nature, as a friend. These lines state his promise to the refugee. The list of loved ones in line 4 leads into the next lines: gathering one's attachments to all these into one cord tied to Ram's feet.

key_terms.sense: hostile to all that moves and does not move

core_teaching: Whoever has harmed all creation, if he comes to Ram afraid and seeking refuge, Ram makes him like a saint at once.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Bhushundi and Shiva are cited as the authorities on Ram's nature; Shambhu in the middle because both others learned it from him. Knowing Ram's nature makes devotion firm.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (gloss of line 3)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'taji mad moh...' as Ram setting aside the refugee's pride, delusion and deceit, not looking at his faults, and at once making him like a saint.
Names the three who know his nature; the fruit of knowing it is that all three worship him constantly.

practical_reading: Used to show that the way back is open even after doing great harm, when a person comes honestly and afraid of who they have been.
misreadings: Not a claim that consequences or the need to repair harm vanish.
cautions: Translation ends with an incomplete list; do not show the fragment on its own.
speaks_to: fear of being rejected for one's past
not_for: victims of harm, if it is used to excuse the harmer

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 48, chaupai lines 5-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 46. Spans two chaupais and needs line 4 (the list of relations) from the previous verse to make sense.
translation_note: Fine, but the first line depends on the list of relations at the end of rcm.5.46.chaupai.1; the translation's 'all of these' needs that list shown with it.
context: Ram is telling Vibhishan his nature. After the promise to the refugee and a list of relations (mother, father, brother, son, wife, body, wealth, home, friends, family), he describes the devotee he holds dear. The doha then says such devotees, whether seeking with or without desire, are dear to him.

key_terms.sense: seeing all with an equal eye
as wealth lives in a miser's heart

core_teaching: Gather all your scattered attachments into one strong cord and tie your mind with it to God. Such a person, even-minded and free of elation, grief and fear, lives in Ram's heart the way money lives in a miser's.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Withdraw attachment from all these and place it all in Ram; attachment that was a fault becomes devotion when turned to him. Compares Vinaya Patrika 103 and Kavitavali 7.30.
Attachment is a thin thread that soon breaks; twisted together and tied to the Lord it becomes a cord that cannot break.
Worldly attachment is not dropped all at once; gather it thread by thread, as autumn water dries slowly, and the person gradually becomes free of 'mine'.

practical_reading: Used to reframe love and attachment: not abandoning loved ones, but letting all one's loves be gathered into one devotion that steadies the mind.
misreadings: Not 'give up your family'; the image is of gathering one's loves, not discarding people.
Not a demand to feel no grief or fear at all, instantly.
cautions: 'No grief or fear' can sound like a judgement on someone who grieves.
Even-mindedness as an ideal can be misused to suppress emotions.
speaks_to: seeking a single centre in life
not_for: fresh grief
someone in an unsafe relationship who may hear 'detach and endure'

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 49, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 47: off by two.
context: After Ram's speech on his nature and his dear devotees, Vibhishan answers. Next he asks for pure devotion dear to Shiva. Ram says, though you have no desire, I will crown you, and anoints him king of Lanka with sea water.
core_teaching: Vibhishan admits he came with some lingering desire (understood as kingship of Lanka), but love for Ram's feet has washed it away.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ram had called him 'Lankesh', so Vibhishan knew Ram meant to crown him; he says that wish is gone. Love is a river because the Ganga flows from those feet: it removes the desire and washes the heart clean.
Agrees with Ramkumar that Vibhishan was not a seeker of gain: when Brahma offered a boon he asked only for pure love of the Lord's feet.

practical_reading: Used to show honesty about mixed motives: we often come to good things for partly selfish reasons, and love can transform those reasons.
misreadings: Not a claim that having had a selfish motive invalidates the turning.
speaks_to: desires fading in a larger love

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 50, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 48: off by two.
context: Ram has crowned Vibhishan. Ravana's spies are noticed. At the shore, Ram asks Sugriva and Vibhishan how to cross the deep ocean. Vibhishan answers. Ram agrees and sits on the shore in prayer to the ocean for three days.

key_terms.sense: able to dry up countless oceans

core_teaching: Even when you have the power to force a way, right conduct says ask first, humbly.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Sugriva stays quiet, since his last advice was overruled; Vibhishan answers. Ram asked as a man, Vibhishan answered knowing his divinity, like Jambavant and the sages elsewhere. As a king of Raghu's line, Ram should honour proper conduct.
Glosses the policy with Dohavali 433: if honey will kill, why give poison; that is, first try conciliation.

practical_reading: Used in conflict and negotiation: try the gentle way first, even from a position of strength.
misreadings: Not a rule of endless appeasement; the sequel shows firmness after patience is ignored.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 57 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says 5.55; the label already notes Gita Press 5.57.
attribution_note: Speaker field is blank for listener; Ram is the speaker of the last line, narration otherwise.
translation_note: Fine.
context: For three days Ram has sat on the shore asking the ocean for a way. Ravana's spy Shuka has just been released. The ocean does not appear. Ram speaks in anger and calls for his bow. When he aims, the ocean appears, begs pardon and tells him how to build the bridge.

key_terms.sense: without some fear there is no regard

core_teaching: After three days of patient asking, Ram sees the ocean will not listen to courtesy and shows anger, since an unfeeling party responds only to firmness.

commentaries.gist: Valmiki 6.21.14-16: calm, forgiveness, straightness and kind speech are taken as weakness by the unworthy; fame cannot be won by conciliation alone.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Three days because a pilgrim stays three nights at a tirtha. He shows anger first in words so the ocean may come without the arrow; mercy remains in his heart, and the anger is shown, not felt.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The ocean's dullness is that it ignored Ram first and came only after provoking his anger.

practical_reading: Used for dealing with someone who ignores repeated, reasonable requests: patience first, then clear firmness, and forgiveness the moment they respond.
misreadings: Not a rule for close relationships or for parenting by fear.
Not permission to intimidate; the firmness follows real patience and ends in forgiveness.
cautions: The proverb 'bhay binu hoi na priti' is often misused to justify fear-based control in families; our data already avoids using it.
speaks_to: a party that keeps ignoring polite requests
when niceness is taken for weakness
not_for: anyone in an abusive or controlling relationship
parenting
partners and close friends

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 58, chaupai lines 1-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says 5.56; the text spans three chaupais.
context: Right after the doha on three days of patient asking, Ram calls for his bow. He then fits a fire arrow; the ocean seethes, then comes as a brahmin, apologises, and advises bridging the sea with Nala and Nila's help.
core_teaching: Some efforts are wasted on the wrong ground: pleading with the stubborn, friendship with the crooked, principles to the miserly, wisdom to the possessive, renunciation to the greedy, calm to the angry, sacred stories to the lustful. All are seed sown on barren land.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: The verbs are left out to show one should not do these at all. Seven faults are barren land and seven virtues the seeds, like the seven grains; all seven faults are found in the ocean.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Stubbornness, crookedness, miserliness, possessiveness, greed, anger and lust block devotion; humility, love, good policy, knowledge, dispassion, calm and holy stories are the matching means.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ram asks for the bow aloud to frighten the ocean into coming; the threat is in speech, not in his heart.

practical_reading: Used to recognise when effort is misplaced: know the ground before you sow, and stop pouring energy into someone who will not receive it.
misreadings: Not a licence to write people off quickly or to bully; this follows three days of patience and ends in forgiveness.
cautions: Labels like 'lustful' and 'angry' can feel like judgements if aimed at the reader.
speaks_to: wasting energy on someone who will not listen
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship who may read 'firmness' as escalation
close family conflicts

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 6, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 8: off by two.
context: The bridge is built and Ram's army has crossed. Ravana, hearing the sea has been bridged, is shaken but boasts. Mandodari takes his hand into the palace and pleads: give up enmity with Ram. After these lines she reminds him of Ram's feats (Madhu, Kaitabh, Hiranyakashipu, Bali, Khara-Dushana) and begs him to return Sita.
core_teaching: Pick fights only with those you can beat by wit and strength; the gap between Ravana and Ram is that of a firefly and the sun.

commentaries.gist: Compares Adhyatma Ramayana (Mandodari: no one can conquer Raghava), Valmiki 6.35 (Malyavan: make peace with an equal or stronger foe) and a Shukraniti verse: make peace with the strong, fight only one you can beat by wit.
'Nath' carries her fear of being left without a protector, which comes true later when the demon women are dragged out and Ravana lies 'like an orphan' on the field.
Everyone Ravana defeated was a jiva; Ram is the lord of all jivas, so there is no comparison.

practical_reading: Used as practical advice on conflict: assess honestly before picking a fight, and do not let pride blind you to what you are up against.
misreadings: Not an argument that one should never stand up to the powerful when one is in the right.
speaks_to: a partner warning against a reckless fight
not_for: someone facing an abuser or bully, who might hear 'never challenge the stronger'

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 10, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 12: off by two.
attribution_note: Prahasta as Ravana's son follows the Manas (Ravana calls him 'sut'). In Valmiki Prahasta is Ravana's commander, not his son.
translation_note: Fine. The second line is narration, not Prahasta.
context: Ravana asks his court for counsel; his ministers flatter him. His son Prahasta says the flatterers will ruin him and urges sending Sita back with a messenger. Ravana insults him harshly ('a bamboo root has sprouted a ghamoi weed'). Prahasta says this line and goes home. The second line is narration: evening comes and Ravana, looking at his twenty arms, goes to his palace, where a dance performance is underway.

key_terms.sense: in the grip of death, doomed

core_teaching: Good advice does not take with one who is doomed, just as medicine does not help a patient already in death's grip. Ravana goes off admiring his own arms.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani (via Manas Piyush vol. 6)
commentaries.gist: He who is seized by death gets no benefit from even good medicine; so Ravana hears good counsel but does not accept it, because he is doomed.
Valmiki uses the same image for Vibhishan's and Maricha's rejected advice: Ravana, driven by time, would not take good counsel, like a dying man refusing medicine (Valmiki 3.40, 6.16, 6.17).
Compares Malyavan's earlier exits: each honest adviser leaves after harsh words, as Prahasta does here.

practical_reading: Used to accept that some people will not take advice however good it is; you can say it once, clearly, and step away.
misreadings: Not a reason to give up on people quickly or to call anyone 'doomed'.
cautions: 'In death's grip' language is sensitive for someone with a seriously ill relative.
not_for: someone whose relative is terminally ill or refusing treatment, where the medicine image may wound

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 18 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 19: off by one.
context: Ram sends Angad as envoy to Ravana. On the way into Lanka Angad meets Ravana's son, who picks a fight, and kills him; word spreads and no one dares stop him. He reaches the door of Ravana's court. Next Ravana laughs and has him brought in.

key_terms.sense: the door of the court (Pt. Ramkumar)
steady, brave, a mass of strength

core_teaching: Angad walks alone into the enemy's court remembering Ram, fearless as a lion, steady and strong.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: 'Darbar' here means the door of the court; he is called in only later. Since everyone had seen the prince killed, no one stopped him, they only showed the way.
A lion walks a little, stands, looks around fearlessly and walks on; 'sinha thavani' expresses that fearlessness.
He looks this way and that for someone to announce him. 'Dhir' because killing the prince did not shake him; 'bir' because ready for battle.

practical_reading: Used before walking into a hard room alone, such as an interview, a hearing or a confrontation: recall what you stand for, and carry yourself with calm courage.
misreadings: Not a model of aggression; the calm is the point.
cautions: The surrounding story includes a killing on the way in.
speaks_to: representing others in a hostile setting

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand sortha 17(kha) (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says 19 sortha 3: wrong doha number.
attribution_note: Speaker is Angad's inner thought, narrated. Fine.
context: Ram has asked his council what to do; Jambavant advises sending Angad as envoy, and Ram tells Angad to do what serves Ram's purpose and Ravana's good. Angad bows, rises and says that whoever Ram favours becomes a sea of virtues (sortha 17 ka). This second sortha is his inner thought. Then he sets out for Lanka.
core_teaching: Angad understands the mission is already certain of success; Ram is simply honouring him by sending him. The thought fills him with joy.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Answers Ram's praise of him as 'home of wit, strength and virtue': whoever Ram favours becomes a sea of virtues.
'As bichari' marks this as an inner thought; joy and zeal are the companions of heroic sentiment and signs of coming success.
Ram's grace on Hanuman earlier brought him fame; Angad sees that he too is being given the chance to earn honour.

practical_reading: Used for doing a task without ego: the outcome does not hang on you alone; being trusted with it is itself the gift.
misreadings: Not an excuse for low effort ('it will happen anyway'); Angad goes and acts boldly.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 34(kha) in the Gita Press edition. Manas Piyush prints it as doha 33 and notes the doha before it (34 ka) is absent from the Kashiraj manuscript.
context: Angad, enraged by Ravana's taunts, plants his foot in the court and vows that if anyone can move it, Ram will turn back and he forfeits Sita. Meghnad and many warriors try and fail. This doha closes the scene. Then Ravana himself rises to grab the foot, and Angad tells him to grasp Ram's feet instead.

key_terms.sense: does not abandon what is right

core_teaching: The monkey's foot stayed planted and the enemy's pride drained away, just as a good person's mind does not let go of right conduct however many obstacles arise.

commentaries.gist: Two readings: the foot does not leave the ground, or the ground does not let go of the foot (fearing for its daughter Sita), which Pt. Ramkumar mentions; the grammar favours the first.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Two images are paired: the deluded man who cannot uproot the tree of delusion, and the saint whose mind holds to dharma despite obstacles, showing strength on both sides.
Kavitavali Lanka 15-16 describes the foot as if Brahma had made it together with the earth, heavier than Meru.

practical_reading: Used for steadfastness: when pressure piles up to make you drop your principles, stay planted.
misreadings: Not stubbornness for its own sake; it is firmness in what is right.
speaks_to: standing alone in a hostile room

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 61, chaupai lines 3-4 in the current Gita Press edition (dataset); Manas Piyush numbers the same section doha 60, which our id follows.
translation_note: Fine. The listener is the unconscious Lakshman; the speech is a lament.
context: Lakshman has been struck down by Meghnad's shakti. Hanuman has gone for the herb and promised to return before dawn. Half the night has passed and he has not come. Ram lifts Lakshman to his chest and laments as an ordinary man would. Next he asks where that love has gone and says he would rather lose wife than brother. Then Hanuman arrives.
core_teaching: Ram, holding his unconscious brother, remembers his gentleness and all he gave up and endured for Ram's sake.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: 'Anuj' carries the thought that the younger should die after the elder. Quotes Hanuman Nataka: you ate after me and slept after me, will you now leave life before me?

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki and Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Valmiki 6.101: rise, you used to console me when I wandered grieving in forests. Gitavali 6.5 gives a parallel lament.
Lakshman came to the forest because he could not bear to see Ram suffer, as his mother Sumitra had told him.

practical_reading: Used to honour the people who have given things up for us: remembering their gentleness and sacrifice, especially when we fear losing them.
misreadings: Not a reason to demand sacrifice from loved ones.
cautions: Speaks over a gravely injured brother; the scene may be hard for someone keeping vigil by a dying relative, though Lakshman is revived.
speaks_to: keeping vigil over a sick loved one
gratitude to a sibling or caregiver
not_for: fresh bereavement, if the revival is not mentioned
someone whose loved one did not recover
